title: A Multidimensional Arithmetical Ontology for High-Parameter Cytometry: Gaussian Primes and Cryptographic Hashing for Cell Population Standardization
summary: Background. The rapid expansion of high-dimensional single-cell technologies has outpaced the development of standardized metadata infrastructure. Current text-based ontology for cell populations and gating strategies lacks computational rigor, hindering process automation and cross-study reproducibility. Our previous frameworks, the Prime Population System (PPS) and the Unique Gating Identifier (UGI), proposed arithmetical solutions but were limited by biological fragility (no inherent link between a protein and its structural isoforms) and by computational bottlenecks caused by exponential integer growth. Objective. To develop a scalable, multidimensional arithmetical ontology that unambiguously identifies cell populations and hierarchical gating strategies. Methods. We transition the marker dictionary from the one-dimensional real axis (R) to the complex plane of Gaussian integers (a+bi). The reviewed human proteome of the UniProt Knowledgebase is paired with Gaussian primes satisfying a > b > 0. Each protein receives a contiguous reserved block of 64 primes: slot 0 addresses the protein with isoform unresolved, and slot k addresses UniProt isoform k, the slot index being read directly off the accession. Carbohydrate epitopes, which have no UniProt entry, are paired through the CD nomenclature instead: in a CD region beyond the 80,000 blocks reserved for the proteome, each CD number receives a block of 1,024 primes, with the slot read off the suffix of the designation. A bipartite encoding represents positive (a+bi) and negative (b+ai) expression states through Conjugate Pair Symmetry. To avoid the integer explosion of Godel exponentiation, hierarchical gating sequences are held as vectorized arrays of complex numbers and compressed by SHA-256 deterministic hashing. Results. Pairing against the human proteome assigns 53,296 identifiers, 20,431 protein-level and 32,865 isoform-level. Every isoform description resolves under a single rule, including the 329 descriptions whose accession prefix differs from the entry that cites them. The 19 carbohydrate designations of the CD list, CD57 among them, receive identifiers in the CD region. Localized vectorization with SHA-256 hashing yields immutable 64-character hexadecimal fingerprints for entire gating strategies, resolving the integer explosion problem. Conclusion. By combining Gaussian primes with hashing, Gaussian Prime Cytometry provides a scalable, computationally lightweight and biologically accurate identifier system. The system eliminates nomenclature ambiguity and facilitates machine learning applications and centralized global cytometry databases.

title: CCIDeconv: Hierarchical model for deconvolution of subcellular cell-cell interactions in single-cell data
summary: Cell-cell interaction (CCI) underlies several fundamental biological processes, including development, homeostasis and disease progression. Subcellular spatial transcriptomics (sST) provides an opportunity to examine whether CCI-associated signals show compartment-specific patterns within cells. Assessing CCI at subcellular level can help us gain insights into the distinct pathway activation and signalling patterns. We developed a novel approach that deconvolutes CCI into subcellular CCI (sCCI) information from non-spatial single-cell transcriptomics (scRNA- seq) based CCI using a modified CellChat-derived communication score. By estimating communication scores separately for cytoplasmic and nuclear compartments, we identified compartment-associated sCCI. We then deconvolved whole-cell communication scores into subcellular compartments using a hierarchical classification and regression framework, which we call CCIDeconv. To ensure biological fidelity, we integrated protein localization data from the Human Protein Atlas in our deconvolution model. Across nine publicly available human sST datasets, leave-one- dataset-out validation achieved a median composite score of 0.75, with mean R2 values of 0.87 and 0.80 for cytoplasmic- and nuclear-associated scores, respectively. Performance without spatial features approached that of spatial models as the number of training datasets increased, supporting application to non-spatial scRNA-seq data. This highlighted the potential for prediction of sCCI from scRNA-seq, given a sufficiently large number of training datasets. Overall, our method can attribute whole-cell CCI to its subcellular compartments, allowing researchers to dissect sCCI patterns and gain insights into the underlying biology of healthy and disease tissues. Keywords Cell-Cell Communication, Single Cell RNA-seq, Predictive Modeling, Bioinformatics, Transcriptomics, Machine Learning

title: Pocket similarity guided selection of protein targets for systematic protein ligand dataset generation
summary: The scarcity of large, diverse, and unbiased protein ligand binding datasets limits the performance of machine learning approaches in drug discovery, particularly for understudied proteins. The Target 2035 initiative aims to address this gap by generating open-access binding data for more than 2,000 human proteins, a goal whose value depends on maximizing the diversity of the selected targets. Because proteins with different folds can share chemically analogous binding sites, we reasoned that pocket similarity, rather than sequence or fold similarity, is the appropriate criterion for selecting representative targets that maximize coverage of the human pocketome. Here, we use PocketVec, an alignment-free descriptor of binding sites, to map the human globular pocketome, identifying 51,535 predicted druggable pockets across 15,559 proteins. A two level hierarchical clustering, first within protein families and then across the whole proteome, grouped these pockets into 1,865 clusters of chemically similar binding sites. After discarding 533 clusters containing pockets with known ligands, we selected the 100 most populated of the remaining 1,332 ligand free clusters and chose two high quality representative pockets per cluster, ranked by their resemblance to known ligand-binding sites. Finally, we implemented two complementary prioritization strategies, one favoring structurally unexplored proteins and the other proteins amenable to experimental follow up, and selected 200 pockets from 100 different clusters from each strategy, with 89 clusters in common. Both selections cover over 10,000 pockets in ~5,600 proteins, approximately 36% of the human proteins with annotated druggable pockets, which represents a 2.8- to 4.4-fold increase in the number of covered pockets, domains, and proteins than random selection baselines. This pocket based framework offers a principled strategy to select diverse targets for Target 2035 and other large scale protein ligand data generation efforts in chemical biology.

title: An auditable harness for biomolecular dynamics simulations by AI agents
summary: AI agents now generate biological hypotheses faster than they can be tested. Hypotheses stated at the atomic level can be examined with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. For new questions without a reference, trust in an agent-run simulation rests on a tool-written process record, not the agent's account. Existing MD agents leave this record to the language model. Here we present MDClaw, a harness whose validating tools and directed acyclic graph (DAG) check stages before execution and record every simulation stage. On MDDataBench, which grades outputs against deposited simulations, four open-weight models with MDClaw passed all three runs on 81-100% of 31 test systems. The DAG complements this outcome check. An ablation without the DAG revealed 11 successful runs that had skipped minimization or equilibration, or simulated a different structure. MDClaw carried questions from human and AI scientists through simulation to trajectories traceable to their inputs and settings.

title: A Complete Three-Dimensional Spiral Ganglion Neuron Map in a Human Adult using a Deep Learning Pipeline
summary: The quantity and distribution of spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs) greatly influence speech and hearing ability. Historically, approaches to quantify SGNs from archival human temporal bones (TBs) have utilized only every 10th section to estimate the total SGN count. The current study evaluates a novel deep-learning pipeline for SGN quantification to produce the first complete three-dimensional SGN map of the human cochlea using every tissue section. The reconstruction is based on one adult human cochlea in which all 421 consecutive, 20 um thick, celloidin-embedded sections were H&E stained, mounted and digitized. SGN nuclei were manually labeled in training sections which were subsequently used to create UNet++ models for SGN detection. These models were then applied to all other sections and compared to manual counts by three experienced histopathologists. After quantification, serial sections were aligned and SGNs were assigned percent distances along Rosenthal's canal and characteristic frequencies using a modified Greenwood formula. Models to automatically identify SGN nuclei from digitized tissue sections performed with great accuracy: SGNs were counted in 191 sections with 97% accuracy compared to manual counts. When tissue sections were systematically omitted, counting only every 10th section was determined sufficient to ensure a median inferred total count accuracy of 98%. We present a new, flexible machine learning pipeline for identifying SGNs in digitized human TBs. Further, we show the first full 3D visualization of all 27,880 SGNs in an adult human cochlea, with associated tonotopic maps and basal-to-apical SGN distributions.

title: RNA Small-Molecule Binding-Site Prediction by Integrating RNA Language Models and Structural Geometry
summary: RNAs are emerging as promising therapeutic targets, and small-molecule binding can modulate their structure and function, creating opportunities for therapeutic development. Accurate identification of RNA small-molecule binding sites is therefore important for understanding RNA-ligand interactions and facilitating RNA-targeted drug discovery. However, the structural complexity of RNA and the limited availability of experimentally characterized RNA-ligand complexes pose challenges for computational binding-site prediction. In this study, we propose RSMBind, a graph attention-based deep learning framework for nucleotide-level prediction of RNA-small molecule binding sites. The model integrates geometric descriptors of the local three-dimensional environment with pretrained RNA language model embeddings to capture complementary structural and sequence information. We investigate three pretrained RNA language models RNA-BERT, ERNIE-RNA and RNA-FM and assess the contributions of sequence representations and geometric features through feature-level ablation experiments. The model is developed using the TR60 and HARIBOSS datasets and evaluated on four independent benchmark datasets: RB9, TE18, TL12 and JL10. RSMBind achieves the highest MCC among the compared methods on three of the four benchmarks, with relative improvements of 17.1% on RB9, 7.2% on TL12 and 16.0% on JL10 over the best previously reported results, while achieving competitive performance on TE18. Furthermore, RSMBind retains predictive capability when using only pretrained RNA language model embeddings, highlighting their potential utility when explicit tertiary structural features are unavailable. Structural analysis indicates differences in prediction performance across RNA structural regions, with loop-associated binding sites generally being captured more effectively than those embedded within stem regions. Additionally, 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations of selected RNA-ligand complexes provide insights into the relationship between predicted binding probabilities and dynamic ligand proximity, further highlighting the role of conformational dynamics in evaluating structure-based predictions. The source code is available at [ https://github.com/sharma-nandita/RSMBind].

title: Unsupervised Clustering Enables Cohort-Specific Variant Recalibration in Crops
summary: Trait discovery in crops require reliable marker datasets, yet variant discovery remains constrained by the lack of standardised, high-confidence reference resources. Publicly available plant genomic resources often rely on outdated reference genomes, heterogenous pipelines, and generic variant hard-filtering thresholds derived from human studies. Consequently, applying the Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK) Best Practices framework, particularly machine learning-based variant quality score recalibration (VQSR), remains challenging in crops lacking suitable training resources. Here, we present an unsupervised approach for variant quality assessment and generating cohort-specific training resources, enabling integration of VQSR into established GATK workflows without predefined high-confidence training variant sets. Using Brassica napus as a model, we use the Illumina 60k Brassica SNP array to establish a reference-specific truth set for base quality score recalibration (BQSR) and independent benchmarking. Gaussian mixture model (GMM)-based clustering of multidimensional variant annotation profiles identifies high-, intermediate-, and low-quality variant classes, which provide flexible training resources without requiring labelled training data. We further validate the approach in diploid Brassica oleracea and hexaploid wheat (Triticum aestivum), representing contrasting population characteristics and genome architectures. Across all three species, GMM-based clustering consistently identifies informative quality classes and enables cohort-specific recalibration of both SNPs and insertion-deletions (INDELs). Comparison with conventional hard filtering reveals discordant pass/fail classifications for up to 46.4% of SNPs and 37.8% of INDELs across evaluated cohorts, demonstrating that the approaches capture distinct aspects of variant quality. Our results establish unsupervised variant classification as transferable strategy for generating cohort-specific VQSR resources, extending established GATK workflows to crops lacking comprehensive genomic resources.

title: Catalytic domain-lipid interactions negatively regulate RhoA signaling by modulating conformational dynamics
summary: RhoA belongs to the Ras superfamily of small GTPases, regulates cytoskeletal actin organization and cell motility, and is implicated in cancer metastasis and neurodegenerative diseases. It is predominantly anchored to the cytosolic side of the plasma membrane (PM) via its prenylated C-terminus, but little is known about its PM organization, dynamics, and lipid interactions. In this work, we used extensive atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and simulations-guided experiments to study the molecular details and functional consequences of RhoA membrane targeting, interactions and dynamics. We found that both GDP- and GTP-bound RhoA adopt a well-defined, stable membrane organization and binding mode irrespective of initial conditions and bilayer lipid composition. RhoA membrane organization is determined by hydrophobic interaction of the prenylated C-terminus with the membrane, and a previously unknown, critical role of electrostatic interactions between cationic residues on the G-domain and N-terminus with anionic lipids in the PM. N-terminal interactions are mediated by a polybasic patch including residues R5, K6, and K7, and substitution of these residues with Ala increased RhoA-mediated F-actin accumulation and effector activation in cells. MD simulations suggest that the triple mutant retains the global membrane organization of wild type RhoA but alters key protein-lipid interactions. Specifically, we observe a loss of cooperative lipid engagement involving the polybasic patch and Switch II residues with amine-bearing lipids, and a rerouting of intra-protein dynamic networks that primes Switch I for effector recognition. These results suggest that the membrane serves not just as a scaffold but also as an allosteric partner of RhoA to fine-tune intra-protein dynamics in a functionally relevant manner.

title: REVEAL: RNA Ensemble Validation and Exploration with AI-guided Landscapes
summary: Capturing the sparsely populated but functionally important, excited states of RNA remains a central challenge for molecular simulation, because the underlying transitions are rare events that unbiased molecular dynamics cannot reach from a single starting structure. Here we introduce REVEAL (RNA Ensemble Validation and Exploration with AI-guided Landscapes), a workflow that couples generative secondary structure sampling, secondary structure conditioned tertiary structure prediction with trRosettaRNA2, unbiased molecular dynamics and Markov state modeling. Using only the sequence of the engineered HIV-1 TAR mutant, in which the excited state ES2 is the dominant conformation, we show that REVEAL captures the reversible ES2 to GS register shift from 6.8 s of aggregate unbiased sampling across 34 seeds, recovering both basins, the intermediate states, and correctly identifies ES2 as the dominant state, consistent with the design of the construct. In contrast, molecular dynamics seeded from the ES2-dominant HIV-1 TAR mutant NMR ensemble remains trapped in ES2 despite substantially longer aggregate simulation time, and sequence-only ensemble predictors (AlphaFold3, Boltz-2, ESMFold2, OpenFold3 and Protenix-v2) place every structure near the ground state and invert the experimentally observed population ordering. The information content of the seed ensemble, rather than the total simulation time, determines whether the transition is sampled. We further introduce ''population-weighted consensus score'' (PWCS) that ranks conformers by how representative they are of the equilibrium ensemble directly from the simulation data, without experimental restraints and independent of the choice of collective variables. PWCS identifies the dominant state even when low-dimensional representations fail to separate the states. Built entirely from open-source tools, REVEAL provides a transparent and extensible route to RNA conformational ensembles beyond the single-structure paradigm.
